0.title: Strength for the Sake of Others
0.overview:
Few questions confuse our generation more than this one: what does it mean to be a man? Some voices say that manhood is about dominance, toughness and conquest, and that real men never show weakness. Others say that manhood is an outdated idea, that talk of male strength is dangerous, and that the differences between men and women are merely what society has taught us. Meanwhile many men simply drift. They avoid responsibility, retreat into screens and entertainment, and leave the hard work of leading, protecting and building to someone else.

The Bible cuts through all of this by starting somewhere else. Manhood is not something a man invents, proves or earns. It is a gift and a calling from God. So God created man in his own image, in the image of God he created him; male and female he created them (Gen 1:27). Men and women stand side by side as equal bearers of God's image, equal in dignity and equal heirs of grace. And God made them different on purpose, so that together they reflect his goodness in ways neither could alone.

Most of all, the Bible shows us manhood in a person. Jesus Christ is the true man, the one who lived as Adam should have lived. In him we see strength without cruelty and tenderness without weakness. He could drive the money changers out of the temple and take little children in his arms. He faced a mob to protect his friends, wept at a friend's grave and washed his disciples' feet. He said of himself, I am gentle and lowly in heart (Matt 11:29), yet he is also the Lion of the tribe of Judah (Rev 5:5).

A simple summary may help as we begin. Biblical manhood is strength used for the good of others under the lordship of Christ. A godly man receives his life as a gift, works and keeps what God has entrusted to him, protects and provides, leads by serving, and loves as Christ loved.

These studies follow the historic Reformed understanding usually called complementarian: men and women are equal in worth, but God has given them distinct and complementary callings, especially in marriage and in the leadership of the church. Many sincere Christians, usually called egalitarians, read some of the key passages differently. Where those questions arise, the other view is explained fairly. And these studies are not only for married men. Jesus never married, and Paul was single for his whole ministry. Every man, married or single, young or old, is called to live out his manhood before God.

Finally, this is not a checklist for proving yourself. Every man who reads these pages has failed as a man in some way, often deeply. The good news is that Christ came for failed men. There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus (Rom 8:1). Biblical manhood grows out of grace, not guilt.

Six units: (1) Made in God's Image; (2) Adam's Calling and Adam's Failure; (3) Jesus, the True Man; (4) Leading by Serving in the Home; (5) The Man in the Church and in the World; (6) Purity, Work and Finishing Well.

1.title: Made in God's Image: Equal and Different
1.overview:
The story of manhood does not begin with men. It begins with God. On the sixth day of creation God made humanity, and he made us in his own image. So God created man in his own image, in the image of God he created him; male and female he created them (Gen 1:27). The word man here means humanity as a whole, and the verse immediately tells us that humanity comes in two forms: male and female. Both reflect God. Both are given dominion over the earth. Both receive God's blessing. And when God looked at everything he had made, including man and woman together, behold, it was very good (Gen 1:31).

This means two things are true at once. First, men and women are equal. A man is not more human, more valuable or more in God's image than a woman. Any view of manhood that treats women as lesser, as objects or as servants of male desire is not biblical manhood. It is sin. Second, men and women are different, and the difference is good. God did not create one kind of person and then divide it arbitrarily. He created a man and a woman, each with a distinct design, so that they would fit together and complement one another.

Genesis 2 fills in the picture. God forms the man first, places him in the garden to work it and keep it (Gen 2:15), gives him his command, and then says, It is not good that the man should be alone (Gen 2:18). The man was made for relationship and for responsibility. He was not made to live for himself.

For a man today, this is the foundation. Your manhood is not a performance you have to keep proving. It is something God gave you when he made you. You do not become a man by winning, earning or dominating. You grow as a man by receiving God's design and living it for his glory and the good of others.
1.theology:
Equal in dignity: Men and women are equally made in God's image (Gen 1:27), equally fallen in sin, and equally redeemed in Christ. Peter calls wives heirs with you of the grace of life (1 Pet 3:7), and Paul says that in Christ there is no male and female, for you are all one in Christ Jesus (Gal 3:28). Before God, no one is a first-class or second-class Christian because of being male or female.

Different by design: Equality does not mean sameness. Scripture consistently presents men and women as distinct, with different bodies, different roles in bearing and raising children, and, as later units will show, different callings in marriage and in the leadership of the church. Paul holds both truths together: Nevertheless, in the Lord woman is not independent of man nor man of woman; for as woman was made from man, so man is now born of woman. And all things are from God (1 Cor 11:11-12).

Received, not proved: The world tells men that manhood must be proved, by strength, money, sexual conquest or success. The Bible tells men that manhood is received from God. A man who knows he is made in God's image and loved in Christ is free from the endless need to prove himself, and free to spend his strength on others.
1.examples:
Two errors in every age: Just a few generations after Adam, Genesis shows us Lamech, the first man in the Bible to take two wives, boasting to them about killing a young man: If Cain's revenge is sevenfold, then Lamech's is seventy-sevenfold (Gen 4:24). He is manhood turned into violence and pride. At the other extreme is Adam in the garden, standing silently while his wife was deceived. Every age produces both kinds of men: the man who dominates and the man who disappears. Our own age has plenty of both.

A simple test: Ask of your own life: when people are around me, do they feel safer or more afraid? Do the people under my influence flourish or shrink? Strength that makes others fearful is not biblical manhood. Strength that makes others safe, free and able to grow reflects the God who made us.

verseByVerse.quote: So God created man in his own image, in the image of God he created him; male and female he created them. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Notice the rhythm of the verse. Three times it says that God created. The creation of humanity is the climax of the whole account. And twice it says in his own image and in the image of God. To bear God's image means to represent him, to reflect his character and to rule the world on his behalf, like a king's statue that shows who owns the land. Then comes the phrase male and female he created them. God did not make man and then add woman as an afterthought. Both are there in the first description of humanity. Every man must begin here: the woman beside him is his equal before God, and his own manhood is a gift from the same Creator.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD God took the man and put him in the garden of Eden to work it and keep it. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Before there was a wife, a family, a nation or a church, God gave the man a job. To work it and keep it. The first word describes cultivating, making the garden fruitful and productive. The second describes guarding, protecting what God had entrusted. These two callings run through the whole Bible's picture of manhood. A godly man builds and he guards. He works to make things grow, and he protects what is good from harm. Work is not a result of the fall. It was part of paradise. What the fall did was make work frustrating (Gen 3:17). The calling itself is good.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the LORD God said, "It is not good that the man should be alone; I will make him a helper fit for him." (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: This is the first time in the Bible that God says something is not good. Everything else in creation was good, but a man alone was not. God made the man for relationship. The solution God provides is a helper fit for him, one who corresponds to him, like him yet different from him. The word helper does not mean servant or inferior. God himself is called his people's helper: Behold, God is my helper (Ps 54:4). For a man, this verse is humbling. He was not made to be self-sufficient. He needs others, and in marriage he needs his wife. Even a single man needs the fellowship of the church. Isolation is not strength. It is not good.

verseByVerse.quote: There is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither slave nor free, there is no male and female, for you are all one in Christ Jesus. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: This verse is sometimes used to argue that there are no differences at all between men and women in the Christian life. But Paul is not erasing the differences between Jew and Greek, slave and free, or male and female. He is saying that none of these differences affect our standing before God. Every believer is justified by faith in exactly the same way, adopted into the same family and one in Christ Jesus. A Christian man may never think of himself as spiritually superior to a Christian woman. At the foot of the cross, the ground is level. Whatever callings God gives men and women in the home and church, they are callings among equals.

1.reflection:
What messages about manhood did you absorb growing up, from family, friends or culture? Which fit the Bible, and which do not?

Why is it important that the Bible establishes equality between men and women before it speaks of any difference in roles?

Genesis 2:15 describes the man's calling to "work" and "keep". What has God entrusted to you to build and to guard?

Which error are you more prone to: dominating others or disappearing from responsibility? What would repentance look like?

2.title: Adam's Calling and Adam's Failure
2.overview:
To understand what has gone wrong with men, we have to go back to the garden. Before the woman was created, God gave the man a clear command: You may surely eat of every tree of the garden, but of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil you shall not eat (Gen 2:16-17). Adam received God's word first, and with it came the responsibility to hold on to it, to teach it and to protect the garden and his wife from anything that would lead them away from it.

Then the serpent came. It spoke to the woman, twisting God's word and questioning his goodness. She was deceived and ate. And then comes one of the most painful phrases in the Bible: she also gave some to her husband who was with her, and he ate (Gen 3:6). Adam was there. He heard the conversation. He did not speak. He did not step between his wife and the serpent. He did not remind her of God's word. He stood silent, and then he followed her into sin.

When God came into the garden, he called first to the man: Where are you? (Gen 3:9). The ESV notes that in Hebrew you is singular. God held the man responsible. And when Adam answered, he blamed his wife and even God himself: The woman whom you gave to be with me. Passivity, then blame. Men have been repeating that pattern ever since.

The results were devastating. Work became painful and frustrating. The relationship between husband and wife was twisted by conflict. And death entered the world. The New Testament says that sin came into the world through one man (Rom 5:12). Every man inherits Adam's nature. But, as the next unit shows, God did not leave men in Adam's failure. He sent another man.
2.theology:
Responsible for the word: God gave the command to Adam before Eve was created (Gen 2:16-17). This does not mean Eve was less responsible for obeying it. But it does suggest that the man carried a particular responsibility to guard and pass on God's word. Spiritual leadership is not a privilege to enjoy but a weight to carry.

Accountable first: Although Eve ate first, God called to Adam first (Gen 3:9), and the New Testament traces humanity's fall to Adam: by the one man's disobedience the many were made sinners (Rom 5:19). In Scripture, the one who leads is the one who answers for those he leads.

The curse on relationships: God told the woman, Your desire shall be for your husband, and he shall rule over you (Gen 3:16). The ESV notes that for may be read "against" and points to Genesis 4:7, where sin's desire is for you, and you must rule over it. Many understand the curse to describe a struggle: the wife tempted to resist her husband's leadership, the husband tempted to crush her. He shall rule over you describes what sin does to marriage, not what God designed it to be. Harsh male rule is a result of the fall, not a picture of godly manhood.
2.examples:
The silent husband: Many Christian homes today have an Adam in them. He loves his family, but he leaves spiritual matters to his wife. She prays with the children, takes them to church, handles the hard conversations and makes the difficult decisions. He is present but passive. The world may call him easygoing. Genesis calls it Adam's sin.

The harsh husband: Other homes have the opposite problem. The man leads, but he leads by anger, control and intimidation. His family walks on eggshells. He may even quote Bible verses about headship. But he is living out the curse, not the creation. Both men need the same thing: to see themselves in Adam, to repent, and to look to the man who got it right.

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD God commanded the man, saying, "You may surely eat of every tree of the garden, but of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil you shall not eat, for in the day that you eat of it you shall surely die." (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: God's first words to the man were full of generosity: You may surely eat of every tree of the garden. Only one tree was forbidden. God's command was not a burden but a boundary that protected life. Adam's task was to trust God's word and to hold on to it. That is still the heart of a godly man's calling. He does not create his own rules or live by his feelings. He listens to what God has said, believes that God is good, and leads others to trust God's word too.

verseByVerse.quote: So when the woman saw that the tree was good for food, and that it was a delight to the eyes, and that the tree was to be desired to make one wise, she took of its fruit and ate, and she also gave some to her husband who was with her, and he ate. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The woman was deceived by what she saw and desired. But the last phrase of the verse points to the man: her husband who was with her. He was not away at work or out in the field. He was standing there. The tragedy of Adam is not only that he ate, but that he did nothing before he ate. His silence was a choice. Many of the worst failures of men are not loud acts of wickedness but quiet refusals to speak, to act and to protect when it mattered most.

verseByVerse.quote: But the LORD God called to the man and said to him, "Where are you?" (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: This is a question not of information but of invitation. God knew where Adam was. He was calling Adam out of hiding and into accountability. And the ESV notes that you is singular: God addressed the man. Even after Adam's sin, God came looking for him. That is grace. God still calls to men who are hiding, in shame, in addiction, in busyness or in silence: Where are you? The way back begins by answering honestly.

verseByVerse.quote: And to Adam he said, "Because you have listened to the voice of your wife and have eaten of the tree of which I commanded you, 'You shall not eat of it,' cursed is the ground because of you; in pain you shall eat of it all the days of your life; (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: God names Adam's sin precisely: Because you have listened to the voice of your wife and have eaten of the tree of which I commanded you. The problem was not that Adam listened to his wife. Wise husbands listen to their wives. The problem was that he listened to her instead of to God. And the result was that cursed is the ground because of you. Adam's work, the very place of his calling, became painful. Men still feel this curse in frustration, failure and exhaustion at work. But in Christ the curse is broken, and work done for him is never in vain.

2.reflection:
Adam was "with her" and said nothing. Where are you tempted to be present but passive in your home, church or friendships?

Why do you think blame comes so naturally to men after failure? How does the gospel free us from the need to blame?

How does it change the way you read Genesis 3:16 to see "he shall rule over you" as a description of sin rather than a command?

God asked, "Where are you?" If he asked you that question today, what would an honest answer be?

3.title: Jesus, the True Man
3.overview:
If Adam shows us what went wrong with manhood, Jesus shows us what manhood was meant to be. Paul calls him the last Adam (1 Cor 15:45). He is the new head of a new humanity, the man who succeeded at every point where Adam failed.

Adam was tested in a garden full of food and fell. Jesus was tested in a barren wilderness after forty days without food and stood firm, answering Satan with God's word: It is written, 'Man shall not live by bread alone' (Luke 4:4). Adam grasped at what God had forbidden. In another garden, Gethsemane, Jesus surrendered to what God had willed: Nevertheless, not my will, but yours, be done (Luke 22:42). Adam stood silent while his wife was deceived. When soldiers came to arrest Jesus, he stepped forward: I told you that I am he. So, if you seek me, let these men go (John 18:8). He put himself between his friends and danger.

Look at the variety of Jesus' manhood. He worked with his hands for years as a carpenter (Mark 6:3). He spoke with authority that silenced his enemies. He was indignant when his disciples kept children away, and then he took them in his arms and blessed them (Mark 10:16). He wept openly at the grave of his friend Lazarus (John 11:35). He knelt and washed his disciples' feet. And he went to the cross, not as a victim overpowered, but as a man laying down his life for others.

This is the model for every man. Jesus shows that true strength is not the power to take but the power to give. And he is not only our model. He is our Savior. No man can copy Jesus by effort alone. We need his forgiveness for our failures and his Spirit to make us like him.
3.theology:
The last Adam: Scripture presents two representative men. For as by the one man's disobedience the many were made sinners, so by the one man's obedience the many will be made righteous (Rom 5:19). Every man is either in Adam or in Christ. Biblical manhood is not first about behavior but about union with Christ, the true man.

Strength under control: Jesus describes himself as gentle and lowly in heart (Matt 11:29). Gentleness is not weakness. It is strength that is held in check and used for the good of others. The same Jesus who is gentle with the broken is the conquering Lion of the tribe of Judah (Rev 5:5). A godly man is not either tough or tender. He is both, at the right time and in the right way.

Power used to serve: Jesus had all authority, and he used it to kneel with a towel and basin (John 13). He taught that the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve (Mark 10:45). In God's kingdom, authority is measured by how much a man gives, not by how much he gets.

Grace for failed men: Jesus understands male weakness from the inside. He in every respect has been tempted as we are, yet without sin (Heb 4:15). And he restores failed men. Peter denied him three times, and Jesus asked him three times, do you love me?, and then gave him a new calling: Feed my sheep (John 21:17).
3.examples:
Two gardens: In Eden, a man stood silent while evil came for the one he should have protected. In Gethsemane, a man stepped forward and said, in effect, "Take me, and let them go." Every Christian man lives between those two gardens. By nature we are Adam. By grace we are being made like Christ.

Men who cry: Many men have been taught that tears are weakness. Yet the shortest verse in the Bible is Jesus wept (John 11:35), and he wept at the grave of a friend. The strongest man who ever lived was not ashamed to grieve. Biblical manhood does not mean hiding every emotion. It means feeling rightly and acting faithfully.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus it is written, "The first man Adam became a living being"; the last Adam became a life-giving spirit. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Paul sets two men side by side. The first man Adam became a living being. He received life from God. The last Adam became a life-giving spirit. Christ gives life to others. This is the heart of the gospel for men. The first Adam passed on sin and death to all his children. The last Adam gives new life to all who belong to him. A man does not become godly by trying harder to be a better Adam. He becomes godly by being joined to Christ and receiving his life.

verseByVerse.quote: If I then, your Lord and Teacher, have washed your feet, you also ought to wash one another's feet. For I have given you an example, that you also should do just as I have done to you. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Jesus had just done a slave's job, washing the dusty feet of his disciples, including the one who would betray him. Then he explained: I have given you an example. Notice that he calls himself your Lord and Teacher. He did not stop being Lord when he knelt. His authority was expressed in service. That is how Christian men are to lead. The husband, the father, the elder and the boss are not above the towel and the basin. The more authority a man has, the lower he should be willing to kneel.

verseByVerse.quote: Take my yoke upon you, and learn from me, for I am gentle and lowly in heart, and you will find rest for your souls. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Jesus invites weary people to come to him because of the kind of man he is: gentle and lowly in heart. The world does not usually admire those qualities in men. But notice that Jesus says this while calling people to take his yoke, to submit to his authority. He is a gentle King, not a weak one. For men, this verse is both a comfort and a pattern. Jesus is gentle with our failures, and he calls us to be gentle with others. The men who are safest to be around are those who have learned from him.

verseByVerse.quote: For we do not have a high priest who is unable to sympathize with our weaknesses, but one who in every respect has been tempted as we are, yet without sin. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Jesus faced the same temptations every man faces: to lust, to grasp at power, to give in to anger, to run from pain, to take the easy way. He faced them in every respect, and he never once gave in. That means he is not a distant example who cannot understand. He is a high priest who can sympathize with our weaknesses. When a man is struggling with temptation, he does not need to hide from Jesus. He can come to the one who knows the fight and has already won it.

3.reflection:
Compare Adam in Genesis 3 with Jesus in John 18:4-8. What does each teach about how a man responds to danger?

Jesus is both "gentle and lowly" and "the Lion of the tribe of Judah." Which of these do you need to grow in most?

Read John 13:1-17. What would washing feet look like in your home, workplace or church this week?

How does knowing that Jesus was tempted "in every respect" change the way you come to him in your struggles?

4.title: Leading by Serving: The Man in His Home
4.overview:
Nowhere is a man's character more clearly seen than at home. It is easy to be admired by colleagues or friends who see only the best of us. The people who live with us see the truth. That is why Scripture speaks so directly to husbands and fathers.

The central verse is Ephesians 5:25: Husbands, love your wives, as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her. Paul does describe the husband as the head of his wife (Eph 5:23). But he immediately defines that headship by the cross. The husband's model is not a king on a throne but a Savior on a cross. His leadership is measured by his sacrifice. Paul adds elsewhere, Husbands, love your wives, and do not be harsh with them (Col 3:19), and Peter tells husbands to live with their wives in an understanding way, showing honor to them (1 Pet 3:7).

A godly husband and father leads spiritually: he takes responsibility for the spiritual health of his home, prays with and for his family, and brings them to God's word. He protects: he guards his family from harm, physical, emotional and spiritual. He provides: he works to meet his family's needs, for if anyone does not provide for his relatives, and especially for members of his household, he has denied the faith (1 Tim 5:8). And he nurtures his children: Fathers, do not provoke your children to anger, but bring them up in the discipline and instruction of the Lord (Eph 6:4).

Christians disagree about how to understand headship. Complementarians, whose view these studies follow, believe God gives husbands a real, loving responsibility to lead, which wives are called to support. Egalitarians point to Ephesians 5:21, submitting to one another out of reverence for Christ, and understand marriage as a partnership of mutual submission without a distinct leadership role for the husband. Both agree on what matters most: a husband must love sacrificially, and no man may ever use Scripture to justify control or abuse.
4.theology:
Headship as responsibility: Paul writes that the head of every man is Christ, the head of a wife is her husband, and the head of Christ is God (1 Cor 11:3). Notice that Christ himself is under the headship of the Father, yet equal to him. Headship does not imply superior worth. It describes an order of responsibility and love. A husband will answer to God for how he has led and loved his wife.

Mutual submission and headship: Ephesians 5:21 calls all believers to submit to one another. Many complementarians understand this as the general call to humility that Paul then applies in specific ways: wives to husbands, children to parents, servants to masters (Eph 5:22-6:9), each relationship with its own shape. In every case, the one with more responsibility is called to the greater self-giving. No Christian husband is exempt from humility.

Protection and provision: When Nehemiah's builders were threatened, he told the men, Remember the Lord, who is great and awesome, and fight for your brothers, your sons, your daughters, your wives, and your homes (Neh 4:14). A godly man takes the dangers facing his family seriously, and he works hard to provide. Where wives also work outside the home, as the capable woman of Proverbs 31 did, the husband's responsibility to see that his household is cared for remains.

Fathers as a picture of God: As a father shows compassion to his children, so the LORD shows compassion to those who fear him (Ps 103:13). Children often learn what God is like from their fathers. A father who is harsh, absent or unpredictable makes it harder for a child to trust the heavenly Father. A father who is present, patient and firm gives his children a living picture of God's love.
4.examples:
What spiritual leadership looks like on a Tuesday: It rarely looks dramatic. It looks like a man who suggests praying together before bed, even when it feels awkward. A man who says to his wife, "I was wrong; please forgive me," before she has to ask. A man who reads a Bible story with his children, gets the family to church when everyone is tired, notices when his wife is overwhelmed and takes something off her plate, and asks her what she thinks before making a big decision. Leadership in the home is mostly initiative, humility and consistency.

When headship is twisted: Tragically, some men use the Bible's teaching on headship to control, intimidate or abuse their wives and children. This is a grievous sin against God and a lie about Christ, who never bullied his bride. Scripture says plainly, do not be harsh with them (Col 3:19). Anyone living in an abusive home should seek safety and help, including from church leaders and, where there is danger or crime, from the authorities. Headship never requires a wife or child to submit to abuse or to sin.

verseByVerse.quote: Husbands, love your wives, as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her, (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Paul could have told husbands to love their wives as much as they are loved by them, or as much as they deserve. Instead he gives an impossible standard: as Christ loved the church. Christ loved his bride when she was unlovely, unfaithful and far from him. He gave himself up for her, all the way to death. A husband who takes this verse seriously will never ask, "What am I getting out of this marriage?" He will ask, "What can I give?" And he will quickly discover that he cannot love like this in his own strength. He will need to go to the cross himself, for forgiveness and for power.

verseByVerse.quote: Husbands, love your wives, and do not be harsh with them. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: This is one of the shortest instructions to husbands in the Bible, and one of the most searching. Do not be harsh with them. Harshness can be loud, in anger and shouting, or quiet, in coldness, sarcasm, criticism and withdrawal. Paul names it because it is a particular temptation for men who carry responsibility and feel the pressure of it. A man can be faithful, hardworking and sexually pure, and still be harsh. God cares about the tone of a man's home, not just the rules of it.

verseByVerse.quote: But if anyone does not provide for his relatives, and especially for members of his household, he has denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: These are some of the strongest words in the New Testament: a man who will not provide for his family has denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever. Even people who do not know God usually care for their own. A Christian who refuses that responsibility has contradicted the faith he claims. The verse does not condemn men who cannot work because of illness, disability or circumstances beyond their control. It condemns neglect. God calls men to take the practical needs of their households seriously, as an act of faith.

verseByVerse.quote: Fathers, do not provoke your children to anger, but bring them up in the discipline and instruction of the Lord. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Paul speaks directly to fathers. He gives a warning and a command. The warning: do not provoke your children to anger, whether by harshness, unfairness, constant criticism, broken promises, favoritism or neglect. The command: bring them up in the discipline and instruction of the Lord. Discipline means training and correction. Instruction means teaching. Both are of the Lord: fathers are not raising children to fit their own image but to know Christ. The Christian father's goal is not merely well-behaved children but children who love God.

4.reflection:
What is the difference between leadership that takes and leadership that gives? Where do you see each in your own life?

Colossians 3:19 warns against harshness. In what forms, loud or quiet, might harshness show up in your home?

How would you explain the complementarian and egalitarian understandings of Ephesians 5 to a friend, fairly and kindly?

If you are a father, what are your children learning about God from you? If you are single, how can you support fathers and families in your church?

5.title: The Man in the Church and in the World
5.overview:
Near the end of his first letter to the Corinthians, Paul gives a compact summary of Christian manhood: Be watchful, stand firm in the faith, act like men, be strong. Let all that you do be done in love (1 Cor 16:13-14). Courage and love belong together. A man who is strong without love becomes a bully. A man who is loving without strength becomes useless when the truth is under attack.

In the church, Scripture calls men to spiritual leadership. The New Testament describes the office of elder or overseer, the pastors who shepherd and teach the church, and lists the qualifications. Among them, an overseer must be the husband of one wife (1 Tim 3:2), which the ESV notes may be read "a man of one woman", that is, a man faithful in his sexual life. Paul also writes, I do not permit a woman to teach or to exercise authority over a man, and he grounds this in creation: For Adam was formed first, then Eve (1 Tim 2:12-13).

Complementarians, including the Reformed tradition historically, understand these passages to mean that the office of elder or pastor is reserved for qualified men, while women serve in many other vital ministries. Egalitarians often understand Paul's words as addressing a particular situation in Ephesus, such as false teaching spreading among untrained women, and believe that women may serve in every office. These studies follow the complementarian reading, because Paul roots his instruction in creation rather than in local circumstances. But both sides should agree on this: church leadership is about character and service, not male privilege.

Most men will never be elders. But every Christian man is called to serve. Older men are to disciple younger men (Titus 2:6-8; 2 Tim 2:2). Men need close friendships with other men who will sharpen them (Prov 27:17). And Christian men are to be salt and light in the world: honest at work, courageous for the weak and faithful in their witness.
5.theology:
Qualified, not merely male: The list of qualifications for elders (1 Tim 3:1-7; Titus 1:5-9) is almost entirely about character: self-controlled, hospitable, gentle, not quarrelsome, not a lover of money, managing his household well. Being male is not enough. The church does not need more men in charge. It needs more godly men who serve.

Why creation order: Paul's stated reason for limiting the teaching and authority of elders to men is not that women are less intelligent or less spiritual. It is the order God established in creation (1 Tim 2:13; compare 1 Cor 11:8-9). Complementarians see this as a good design that reflects the relationship between Christ and his church. Egalitarians read the same passages differently, and Christians on both sides love Scripture and seek to obey it.

Men discipling men: What you have heard from me in the presence of many witnesses entrust to faithful men, who will be able to teach others also (2 Tim 2:2). Christianity spreads through relationships. A mature Christian man is not only a learner but a trainer of others.

Brotherhood: The soul of Jonathan was knit to the soul of David, and Jonathan loved him as his own soul (1 Sam 18:1). Deep friendship between men is a gift from God. It is not weakness to need brothers who know your struggles, pray for you and tell you the truth.
5.examples:
The loneliness of men: Many men have plenty of acquaintances and no real friends. They talk about sports, work and news, but no one knows their fears, temptations or doubts. Isolation makes men vulnerable to sin and despair. A practical step: find one or two Christian men and meet regularly to read Scripture, pray and ask honest questions about each other's lives.

Courage in public: Proverbs calls a leader to Open your mouth for the mute, for the rights of all who are destitute (Prov 31:8). Christian men are called to use their strength for those who cannot defend themselves: the unborn, the poor, the abused, the overlooked colleague, the bullied child. Biblical manhood is not loud self-assertion. It is courage spent on others.

verseByVerse.quote: Be watchful, stand firm in the faith, act like men, be strong. Let all that you do be done in love. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Four short commands and one that governs them all. Be watchful: stay spiritually alert. Stand firm in the faith: do not be moved from the truth. Act like men: take responsibility with courage, and do not be childish or cowardly. Be strong: persevere. And then, Let all that you do be done in love. Paul wrote this to the whole church, women included, but the phrase act like men shows that Scripture does associate courage and steadiness with manhood. The final command keeps that courage from becoming harsh. Christian strength is always love in action.

verseByVerse.quote: I do not permit a woman to teach or to exercise authority over a man; rather, she is to remain quiet. For Adam was formed first, then Eve; (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: This is one of the most debated passages in the New Testament, and it deserves careful, humble reading. Paul restricts two things: teaching men and exercising authority over men, most naturally understood in the setting of the gathered church and its leadership. He does not forbid women from teaching altogether, since elsewhere older women are to teach younger women (Titus 2:3-4) and Priscilla helped explain the gospel to Apollos (Acts 18:26). And he gives a reason from creation, not culture: For Adam was formed first, then Eve. For men, this passage is not a trophy but a trust. If God calls qualified men to shepherd his church, they must do it as servants who will give an account.

verseByVerse.quote: Likewise, urge the younger men to be self-controlled. Show yourself in all respects to be a model of good works, and in your teaching show integrity, dignity, (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Paul's instruction for younger men is strikingly simple: be self-controlled. Self-control is the virtue young men most need and most lack: control of anger, appetite, sexual desire, tongue and time. Then Paul tells Titus to Show yourself in all respects to be a model of good works. Young men learn by watching older men. Every Christian man is teaching someone, whether he intends to or not. The question is what his life is teaching.

verseByVerse.quote: Iron sharpens iron, and one man sharpens another. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: When two iron blades are rubbed together, both become sharper. Friction is part of the process. Real friendship between men is not always comfortable. It includes honest conversation, disagreement, rebuke and encouragement. A man who surrounds himself only with people who flatter him will grow dull. A man who welcomes brothers who challenge him will grow sharp and useful for God.

5.reflection:
"Be strong. Let all that you do be done in love." Which half of that command is harder for you, and why?

Why does it matter that Paul grounds his teaching about church leadership in creation (1 Tim 2:13)? How would you answer a friend who holds the egalitarian view, with grace?

Who are the older men investing in you? Which younger men could you invest in?

Do you have a friend who sharpens you? What would it take to build that kind of friendship?

6.title: Purity, Work and Finishing Well
6.overview:
The final unit turns to three battlegrounds where many men win or lose the Christian life: sexual purity, daily work and long-term faithfulness.

First, purity. Job said, I have made a covenant with my eyes; how then could I gaze at a virgin? (Job 31:1). Jesus went further: everyone who looks at a woman with lustful intent has already committed adultery with her in his heart (Matt 5:28). In a world of instant pornography and constant sexual images, this may be the fiercest battle Christian men face. The Bible's strategy is clear: flee youthful passions and pursue righteousness, faith, love, and peace, along with those who call on the Lord from a pure heart (2 Tim 2:22). Run from temptation, run toward godliness, and do not run alone.

Second, work. Whatever you do, work heartily, as for the Lord and not for men (Col 3:23). Work is not merely a way to earn money. It is a way to serve Christ, to love neighbors and to provide for others. Laziness is a sin (Prov 6:6; 2 Thess 3:10). So is making work an idol that consumes a man's family and his soul.

Third, finishing well. Many men start strong and fade. Paul, near his death, could say, I have fought the good fight, I have finished the race, I have kept the faith (2 Tim 4:7). Biblical manhood is not a burst of zeal but a long obedience.

These callings belong to single men as much as married men. Paul says that The unmarried man is anxious about the things of the Lord, how to please the Lord (1 Cor 7:32). Singleness is not a waiting room for manhood. It can be a season, or a lifetime, of undivided devotion to Christ.
6.theology:
Purity as holiness: For this is the will of God, your sanctification: that you abstain from sexual immorality; that each one of you know how to control his own body in holiness and honor (1 Thess 4:3-4). Sexual purity is not only avoiding certain acts. It is honoring God with the body, honoring women as sisters and image-bearers, and keeping sex for the covenant of marriage.

Grace for the fallen: Many men carry deep shame about sexual sin. The gospel does not excuse sin, but it does forgive it. If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness (1 John 1:9). Confession to God, and often to a trusted brother, is the path to freedom.

Work as worship: Work was given before the fall (Gen 2:15), and Christ himself worked as a carpenter. Whether a man is a laborer, a manager, a student or retired, he can do his work as for the Lord, knowing that You are serving the Lord Christ (Col 3:24).

Perseverance: Let us run with endurance the race that is set before us, looking to Jesus (Heb 12:1-2). Men finish well not by gritting their teeth but by keeping their eyes on Christ, who finished his race for them.
6.examples:
The fight for purity in a digital age: Practical wisdom matters. Put filters and accountability on devices. Do not take a phone to bed. Know your danger times, such as late at night, when tired, lonely or stressed. Replace, do not only remove: fill your mind with Scripture and your life with good work and friendship. When you fall, confess quickly to God and to a brother, and get back up. Shame drives men into hiding. Grace brings them into the light.

An old man who finished strong: Caleb, at eighty-five, said to Joshua, I am still as strong today as I was in the day that Moses sent me, and asked for the hardest territory: So now give me this hill country (Josh 14:11-12). He had followed the LORD wholeheartedly for forty-five years. Scripture promises that the righteous still bear fruit in old age (Ps 92:14). Retirement is not the end of a man's calling. Grandfathers, mentors and praying old men are among the church's greatest treasures.

verseByVerse.quote: "I have made a covenant with my eyes; how then could I gaze at a virgin? (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Job did not wait until temptation arrived to decide what he would do. He made a covenant with my eyes beforehand. A covenant is a binding promise. Sexual purity is rarely won in the moment of temptation. It is won by decisions made earlier: where we go, what we watch, what we allow ourselves to look at and think about. Every man needs a settled resolve before God about his eyes.

verseByVerse.quote: So flee youthful passions and pursue righteousness, faith, love, and peace, along with those who call on the Lord from a pure heart. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Paul gives Timothy a two-part strategy. Flee: do not negotiate with sexual temptation, run from it, as Joseph ran from Potiphar's wife. Pursue: chase after righteousness, faith, love and peace. The Christian life is not only saying no. It is saying yes to something better. And notice the last phrase: along with those who call on the Lord from a pure heart. Purity is a team effort. Men who try to fight alone usually lose.

verseByVerse.quote: Whatever you do, work heartily, as for the Lord and not for men, knowing that from the Lord you will receive the inheritance as your reward. You are serving the Lord Christ. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Paul originally wrote these words to slaves, people with the hardest and least rewarding work imaginable. Even there, Paul says, work can be done heartily, as for the Lord. No job is too small to be done for Christ, and no job is too important to be done for yourself. The phrase You are serving the Lord Christ changes everything. A man's real boss is Jesus, and Jesus sees what no manager notices.

verseByVerse.quote: I have fought the good fight, I have finished the race, I have kept the faith. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Paul wrote these words in prison, expecting to be executed soon. Looking back on his life, he describes three things: a fight, a race and a trust. I have fought the good fight: the battle against sin, error and discouragement. I have finished the race: he did not quit. I have kept the faith: he guarded the truth entrusted to him. That is how every Christian man should want his life to end. Not with perfection, for Paul called himself the foremost of sinners, but with faithfulness, held up to the end by the grace of Christ.

6.reflection:
What practical steps have you taken, or should you take, to "flee" sexual temptation and "pursue" righteousness with others?

How would your attitude to your daily work change if you truly believed "You are serving the Lord Christ"?

If you are single, how can you use this season for "undivided devotion" to the Lord? If married, how can you support single men in your church?

Imagine your life at eighty-five. What kind of man do you want to be then, and what habits now will help you get there?
